title: Override clone judiciously
concept: The Cloneable interface was intended as a mixin interface for objects to advertise that cloning is permitted. Unfortunately, it fails to achieve this goal: Cloneable contains no methods, and Object's protected clone method determines whether to return a field-by-field shallow copy or throw CloneNotSupportedException based on whether the class implements the marker interface. This architecture is flawed, complex, and bypasses constructor invocation. In general, copy constructors or copy factories provide a vastly superior alternative to Cloneable.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: What is the best way to provide object copying functionality in modern Java?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: Provide a copy constructor (e.g. `public Yum(Yum yum)`) or copy factory (e.g. `public static Yum newInstance(Yum yum)`). Do not implement Cloneable.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: What is the only valid, idiomatic use of the `clone()` method in Java?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Cloning arrays (e.g. `array.clone()`), where the JVM provides a fast, type-safe copy of identical compile-time type without casting.

quiz.question: What is the design anomaly regarding the `Cloneable` interface in Java?
options: Cloneable does not define a clone() method; instead, it modifies the behavior of Object's protected clone() method
It can only be implemented by abstract classes
It forces all cloned fields to be static
It requires classes to implement Serializable as well

quiz.question: Why does `super.clone()` violate normal Java object lifecycle rules?
options: It allocates and initializes an object without calling any constructor
It runs on the garbage collector thread
It bypasses all private variable visibility rules
It prevents garbage collection of the original object

quiz.question: What happens if a class containing mutable fields uses a simple `(MyClass) super.clone()` without deep copying?
options: A shallow copy is created where both the original and clone share references to the same mutable internal objects
A CloneNotSupportedException is thrown at runtime
All mutable fields are set to null
The compiler throws a ClassCastException

quiz.question: Which of the following is an advantage that copy constructors and copy factories have over `Cloneable`?
options: They don't rely on risk-prone field-copying mechanisms, don't conflict with final fields, and can accept argument types of an interface
They are executed directly by the CPU without bytecode
They automatically serialize objects to JSON
They can clone non-instantiable classes

quiz.question: Why is `clone()` incompatible with `final` fields pointing to mutable objects?
options: A final field cannot be assigned a new deep-copied value inside clone() because final fields can only be assigned in constructors
The compiler forbids final fields in any class implementing Cloneable
final fields are erased by type erasure
final fields are always shared globally across threads

interview_questions.question: Why does Joshua Bloch advise against implementing `Cloneable` in new classes?
interview_questions.model_answer: `Cloneable` is one of the most poorly designed parts of the Java standard library. It is an empty marker interface that alters the behavior of a protected method in `Object`. It constructs objects without calling constructors, conflicts with `final` fields, requires casts and handling checked `CloneNotSupportedException`, and is easily corrupted by shallow copies. Copy constructors and copy factories are strictly superior.

interview_questions.question: A class has `private final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();`. The author attempts to implement `clone()` with deep copying. Why will it fail to compile?
interview_questions.model_answer: In `clone()`, `super.clone()` shallow-copies the `list` reference. To make a deep copy, the clone would need to assign `result.list = new ArrayList<>(this.list);`. But because `list` is marked `final`, re-assigning it outside of a constructor causes a compile error. In effect, `Cloneable` is fundamentally incompatible with normal use of `final` fields.

interview_questions.question: What is a 'conversion constructor' or 'conversion factory', and how is it superior to `clone()`?
interview_questions.model_answer: A conversion constructor takes an interface argument rather than the concrete class (e.g. `public HashSet(Collection<? extends E> c)`). This allows the client to choose the destination implementation type when copying (e.g. copying an `ArrayList` into a `TreeSet`), something `clone()` can never do.

interview_questions.question: When is `clone()` actually recommended and safe to use in modern Java?
interview_questions.model_answer: On primitive or object arrays (e.g. `int[] copy = original.clone()`). For arrays, `clone()` is high-performance, requires no casting, does not throw checked exceptions, and returns an exact replica with identical runtime type.
